meta.blurb: At nine o'clock Grace holds an empty mug in her quiet kitchen. After a lifetime of teaching, she has nowhere to be. Kofi works nights and loses his free hours to his phone. Both find small, real reasons to start the day.
meta.bible: Grace: a retired teacher aged sixty-eight, who lives alone and finds her days empty. Kofi: a man of twenty-four who works nights in a warehouse and spends his free hours on his phone. Dev: Grace's neighbour, who grows tomatoes. Key terms: Reasons, Curiosity, Routine, Commitment, Gentle goals. The book speaks to You in kind, practical, everyday words. It gives general encouragement only and says when to talk to a doctor. Voice: warm, simple, concrete and quietly humorous. No invented studies, numbers or quotes. A reason to get up does not have to be a grand purpose.

B1B2: An alarm clock can wake you up, but it cannot make you want to get out of bed. That wish comes from having a reason, and this book is about finding one.
Almost everyone has mornings when the bed feels like the safest place in the world. One heavy morning is not a problem, but a long run of them is a signal that deserves some attention.
An alarm pushes you out of bed from behind, and pushing is tiring because you have to keep doing it. A good reason works the other way, because it pulls you gently forward.
Grace taught children for forty years, and now she is sixty-eight and retired. Nobody needs her at eight o'clock any more, and the mornings seem terribly long.
Kofi is twenty-four and works nights in a warehouse. By the time he wakes in the afternoon, he reaches for his phone, and three hours later he cannot say what he has actually done.
People often imagine that a reason to get up must be something big. In fact it can be a cup of good coffee, a plant that needs water or a friend who will be waiting.
You do not need one great calling to live well. A few small reasons, each one nothing special alone, can stack together like bricks and hold up a whole day.
Here is a first exercise, and it only needs a pen and some quiet time. Think back over the last year, and write down five things that you honestly looked forward to, even if they seem unimportant.

Next, notice the things that make time disappear, because those are clues too. When you are so interested in something that you forget to check your watch, you have probably found something that matters to you.
Curiosity is one of the best kinds of fuel for a morning. Ask yourself one small question about the world each day, such as why the sky turns pink at sunset, and see where it leads.
One morning a small brown bird lands on Grace's fence, and she realises that she does not know what it is. She borrows a bird book from the library, and the next morning she is awake early to look.
Learning a new skill is rewarding because you can feel yourself getting better. Each time Grace correctly names a bird, she feels a small spark of pride.
Kofi is tired of eating crisps and cold pizza, so he decides to cook one new dish every Sunday. By the third week, he is choosing recipes on Thursday just because he enjoys thinking about it.
There is a special satisfaction in making or mending something with your own hands. Cooking, knitting, gardening and repairing a chair all give you something real to look at when you finish.

Try this simple trick tonight, just before you switch off the light and go to sleep. Put out your favourite cup, a tea bag and perhaps a biscuit, so that the first thing you see tomorrow is something pleasant.
Make your first half hour of the day pleasant. Play some music you like, sit in your favourite chair and drink something warm, and the rest of the morning will feel lighter.
Open the curtains as soon as you get up, and if you can, step outside for a few minutes. Daylight helps the body to understand that the day has begun.

You do not have to run a marathon or join an expensive gym. A ten-minute walk, some stretching or a few steps of dancing in the kitchen often lifts your mood, although it affects people in different ways.
Mornings are much easier after a good night's sleep. Try to go to bed at about the same time each night, and leave your phone on the other side of the room.
Many of us reach for our phone before we are properly awake. If you can wait ten minutes, you will start the day with your own thoughts instead of everyone else's news and opinions.
Grace sees a notice for a Tuesday walking group in the library. She goes, a little nervously, and by the third week the others are asking where she is if she is late.
A colleague invites Kofi to a casual game of football on Saturday afternoons. Kofi says yes, and soon he is going to bed earlier on Friday so that he will not let the team down.
A promise to another person is a powerful reason to get up. When you have said that you will meet someone at ten, you will often go, even on mornings when you would not go for yourself.
Grace asks the librarian if she can read to small children on Thursday mornings. The children wriggle and giggle, and Grace goes home with the feeling that she has been useful.
There is a difference between being needed and being loved, and both can give you a reason to get up. It is worth asking yourself who you could help, and who might enjoy your company.
Put one thing in your week that you really look forward to, such as a swim, a call with a friend or a class. It acts like a post in the ground that the rest of the week is tied to.
Big goals are exciting, but they often fail on tired days. Choose a goal that is so small you cannot fail at it, such as five minutes of walking, and raise it slowly.
A goal that takes a year can feel very distant. A goal you can finish today, such as posting a letter or fixing a shelf, gives you the pleasant feeling of having completed something.
Waiting to feel motivated is a trap, because the feeling often arrives only after you begin. If you do not want to go for a walk, just put on your shoes, and see what happens.
Boredom is a short feeling that passes when you find something to do. A lack of purpose is a deeper feeling that nothing matters, and it needs more careful attention.
Sometimes you are not short of reasons but simply short of sleep. If you have been working hard or sleeping badly, rest first, and then ask yourself again whether you have a reason.
We rush through so much that we forget to taste it. Make one simple pleasure a slow one each day, such as a cup of tea, and give it your whole attention until it is finished.
Children play without asking what it is for, but adults often forget how to do that. We feel that every activity must have a purpose, yet doing something just for fun can fill you with energy.
Grace buys a small box of paints and tries to paint the birds she sees. They look rather strange, but she enjoys the quiet hour of looking and mixing colours, and she is proud of every one.
Many adults avoid new things because they hate being bad at them. Remember that every expert you admire was once a beginner who was willing to look a little foolish.
Dev, Grace's neighbour, grows tomatoes in pots on his balcony, and he checks them every morning. A living thing that needs you gives the day a very gentle kind of structure.
For many people, a dog or a cat is a very good reason to get up in the morning. A pet is a big responsibility, though, so think carefully before you decide, and be honest about what you can manage.
Kofi asks his manager if he can learn to use the stock computer system. A few weeks later he is trusted with new tasks, and the same job feels more interesting than before.
Money worries are real, and they can make everything feel harder. Even so, many of the best reasons to get up, such as a walk, a chat or a library book, cost nothing at all.
Take a calendar and pick one thing to look forward to in each month of the year. They can be small, such as a picnic, a film or a visit, but they give the year some bright landmarks.
A wish is much more likely to happen when it has a date next to it. Ring the day on the calendar, tell a friend about it, and you will feel the pull of it growing as it approaches.
Before you go to sleep, write down three good things that happened that day. They can be tiny, such as a friendly smile or a tasty lunch, and soon you will be looking for them in the daytime.
People are sometimes told that they are too old to begin something new. It is true that some things become harder, but at any age you can learn, make friends and enjoy a fresh start.

Grace begins to give short talks about birds at the library, and people ask her good questions. She realises that she is still a teacher, only now she teaches because she wants to, not because she must.
There will be mornings when you stay in bed, and that is not a disaster. Do not blame yourself, but simply decide that you will try again tomorrow, with one small reason ready.

If you feel that nothing interests you for many weeks, or if your sleep and appetite have changed a lot, please talk to a doctor. Low mood is common and often treatable, and this book is not a replacement for medical advice.
One day Grace and Kofi meet at the bus stop, and Kofi admits that he finds mornings hard. Grace tells him that she does too, and that simple honesty turns out to be a relief for both of them.
A reason that works in spring may fade by autumn. That is normal, so look at your list every few months, drop what has lost its pull and add something new.
Let us gather the ideas into one place before we say goodbye. Look for small reasons, share them with other people, stay curious, set gentle goals and rest when you are tired.
Tonight, before you go to bed, choose one small reason to get up tomorrow and say it out loud. In the morning, the alarm will still ring, but this time you will have something waiting for you.
C1C2: An alarm clock is very good at waking you, yet it has never persuaded anyone that the day ahead is worth entering. That quiet wish to get up comes only from having a reason, something waiting on the other side of the morning that you would honestly like to meet. This book is about finding yours, and about learning to recognise it when it quietly arrives on an ordinary day.

Almost everyone has mornings when the bed feels like the safest place in the world and the day looks like a long, grey corridor. A single heavy morning is nothing to worry about, but a long run of them is a quiet signal, and it deserves some kindness and some attention. We shall come back to that subject near the end of the book, because it matters a great deal and should not be hurried.

An alarm pushes you out of bed from behind, and pushing is tiring because it must be repeated every single morning. A good reason works in the opposite way, drawing you forward like a rope tied to something you want. The difference sounds small, yet it separates people who drag themselves through the day from those who walk.

Grace spent forty years in a school classroom, where every morning came with thirty faces and a hundred small demands. Now she is sixty-eight and retired, nobody needs her at eight o'clock any longer, and the mornings stretch ahead of her like a long, empty hallway. She has plenty of freedom, and more free time than she ever dreamed of as a teacher, but somewhere along the way she has lost her reason.

Kofi is twenty-four and works the night shift in a large warehouse, so his days begin when other people's are already half over. He wakes in the afternoon and reaches for his phone, and three hours later he surfaces without being able to say what he has seen, learned or enjoyed. His precious time has slipped through his fingers like sand, and he can feel the days beginning to blur into one another.

People often imagine that a reason to get up must be something large and important, like a career or a mission. In fact it can be a cup of excellent coffee, a plant that needs watering or a friend who will be waiting at the corner café. Small reasons are not second-rate, because a day is made almost entirely of small moments, and these are the ones we actually live in.

You do not need one overwhelming calling in order to live well, and waiting for one is a good way to waste a decade. A handful of small reasons, none of them impressive on its own, can be stacked together like bricks until they hold up an entire day. A sturdy wall does not require a single enormous stone, and neither does a sturdy life, so begin with whatever bricks you have.

Here is a first exercise, and it needs only a pen and a few quiet minutes. Think back over the last twelve months and write down five things that you honestly looked forward to, however trivial they may seem, for example a certain meal, a certain song or a certain person. Those five things are clues to what pulls you forward, and they are well worth studying before you read on.

Next, pay close attention to the activities that make the hours vanish without your noticing them going. When you are so absorbed in something that you forget to check the clock, forget to be hungry and forget your small worries, you have almost certainly found a thing that matters to you. It need not be useful or impressive, since it is enough that it holds your attention.

Curiosity is one of the finest fuels for a morning, because it makes tomorrow interesting simply by being unfinished. Ask yourself a single small question about the world each day, for example why the sky turns pink at sunset or how a bridge stays up, and let it lead you wherever it wishes. A mind that is busy wondering is rarely bored, and a person who is rarely bored is much more likely to leap out of bed.

One morning a small brown bird lands on Grace's garden fence, and she realises with some embarrassment that she has no idea what it is. She borrows a bird book from the library that afternoon, and the following morning she wakes earlier than usual in order to look out of the window. It is the first time in months that she has had somewhere to be.

Learning something new is rewarding because the progress is visible, even when it is slow. Each time Grace correctly names a bird, she gives herself a small tick in the margin of the book, and the ticks begin to look like a little staircase going up. Improvement, however modest, is one of the most dependable sources of energy there is.

Kofi is tired of living on crisps and cold pizza, so he makes a small resolution to cook one new dish every Sunday. By the third week he has begun choosing recipes on Thursday, simply because he enjoys the anticipation, and his flat smells of onions and spices instead of old takeaway boxes. A weekly project gives the whole week a pleasant slope, so that each day seems to lean gently towards something good.

There is a special kind of satisfaction in making or mending something with your own hands. Cooking, knitting, gardening and repairing a wobbly chair all leave you with something real to look at when you have finished, which is more than can be said for an afternoon of scrolling. The hands seem to do a quiet kind of thinking of their own, while the busy and anxious mind is allowed to take a rest.

Try a simple trick tonight, which is to prepare a small pleasure for the morning before you go to bed. Put out your favourite cup, a tea bag and perhaps a biscuit, so that the very first thing you see tomorrow is an invitation rather than a chore. It costs almost nothing and takes a minute, yet it quite noticeably changes the way in which the day begins.

Make the first half hour of your day as agreeable as you possibly can. Play music that you love, sit in your favourite chair and drink something warm, and the rest of the morning will feel noticeably lighter than it would have done if you had rushed straight into it. A good beginning does not guarantee a good day, of course, but it certainly helps and it is entirely within your power.

Open the curtains the moment you get up, and if you possibly can, step outside for a few minutes of fresh air. Daylight helps the body clock to understand that the day has begun, and many people find that even a short moment in the open makes them feel more awake and a little more hopeful. Gloomy rooms tend to produce gloomy thoughts, and bright ones, on the whole, produce rather brighter ideas.

You do not have to run a marathon, or even go near a gym, in order to benefit from moving your body. A ten-minute walk, a few gentle stretches or a little dancing in the kitchen often lifts the mood and gives people energy, although the effect varies from person to person. The best kind of exercise is simply the kind that you will actually do.

Mornings are far easier to face after a decent night's sleep, and sleep is easier when it follows a regular pattern. Try to go to bed at roughly the same time each evening, and leave your phone charging on the other side of the room, where it cannot tempt you at midnight or ambush you at dawn. A rested mind is a far more generous judge of the day ahead, and it is quite a bit more likely to find a reason.

Many of us reach for the phone before we are properly awake, and the first thing we meet is other people's news, opinions and worries. If you can wait ten minutes, you will begin the day with your own thoughts instead, and you may be surprised at how different the morning feels. The screen will still be there when you are ready for it, and nothing urgent is likely to have happened in the meantime.

Grace notices an advertisement for a Tuesday morning walking group on the library noticeboard, and after a week of hesitation she decides to go. She feels rather nervous at first, but by the third week the other walkers are asking where she is if she is a few minutes late. To be missed, she discovers, is a wonderful reason to turn up, and she had not realised how much she wanted it.

A colleague invites Kofi to join a casual game of football on Saturday afternoons, and after some hesitation Kofi says yes. Within a month he is going to bed earlier on Fridays, eating a proper breakfast and arriving ten minutes early, because he does not want to let his teammates down. Other people can pull us forward when our own motivation is faint, much as a stronger swimmer pulls a tired one towards shore.

A promise made to another person is among the most potent of all reasons, since most of us dislike breaking our word. Once you have agreed to meet someone at ten o'clock, you will frequently go, even on mornings when you would never have stirred for your own sake. Choose modest commitments that you will be glad to have made, and keep them for the quiet satisfaction of being reliable.

Grace asks the librarian whether she might read stories to small children on Thursday mornings, and the librarian looks delighted. The children wriggle, giggle and interrupt, and Grace goes home with the warm, tired feeling of having been useful, a feeling she had quite forgotten she missed. Being of use is a very old and very reliable human pleasure, and it is available to almost everyone at any age.

It is worth noticing that being needed and being loved are two different gifts, and either of them can give a morning its meaning. Ask yourself who might benefit from your skills, and who might simply enjoy your company, because the answers to these questions are often closer than you think. A neighbour, a niece or a lonely stranger might be waiting for exactly you.

Put one thing in your week that you truly look forward to, such as a swim, a call with an old friend or an evening class. It acts like a post in the ground, giving the rest of the week something to be tied to, so that the days lean towards it instead of dissolving into each other. A week without a landmark can feel like a flat and featureless plain, across which it is hard to find any reason to walk.

Big goals are exciting to make and easy to abandon, especially on tired and discouraging days. Choose instead a gentle goal so small that failure is almost impossible, such as five minutes of walking or one page of a book, and raise it slowly as your confidence grows. A habit that succeeds every day will, in the long run, beat an ambition that succeeds only once and then collapses.

A goal that will take a year to reach can feel impossibly distant on an ordinary Tuesday. A goal that can be finished today, such as posting a letter, mending a shelf or phoning a relative, gives you the pleasant sensation of having completed something before bedtime. A string of these small finishes can quietly add up to a good deal of progress.

Waiting until you feel motivated is a trap, because the feeling very often arrives only after you have begun. If you cannot face the idea of a walk, do not think about the whole walk, but simply put on your shoes and open the front door. The smallest piece of a task is usually the one that unlocks all the rest.

Boredom is a restless, temporary feeling that passes as soon as you find something interesting to do. A lack of purpose is quieter and deeper, a feeling that nothing matters very much, and it needs more patient and careful attention than a new hobby. Knowing which of the two you are feeling helps you to choose a suitable response.

Sometimes you are not short of reasons at all but merely short of sleep, and exhaustion can disguise itself very convincingly as despair. If you have been working hard or sleeping badly for a long time, rest first, and only then ask yourself again whether you have a reason to get up. Rest is not the enemy of purpose but its foundation, and nobody builds anything lasting while permanently exhausted.

We rush through so many of our days that we forget to taste them. Choose one simple pleasure, a cup of tea or a piece of fruit or a few minutes in the sun, and make it a slow one, giving it your complete attention from the first sip to the last. A life that is hurried past is a life that is hardly lived, whereas one that is tasted slowly feels remarkably long.

Children play without ever asking what it is for, whereas adults tend to feel that every activity must be productive or at least improving. Yet doing something purely for fun, such as painting badly, singing in the kitchen or building a ridiculous sandcastle, can flood you with energy and good humour. Play is not the opposite of seriousness but its necessary companion, and a person who never plays soon grows rather grey.

Grace buys a small box of watercolour paints and tries to capture the birds she sees from her kitchen window. The results look rather strange, with robins that resemble potatoes, but she loves the quiet hour of looking closely and mixing colours, and she pins every painting to the wall. Enjoyment, she is learning, does not depend on talent, and it grows with every hour spent looking carefully at something you love.

Many adults avoid new activities because they cannot bear to be bad at them, and so they stay safely within the narrow circle of what they already do well. Remember that every expert you admire was once a beginner who was willing to look a little foolish for a while. Awkward beginnings are not signs of failure but the ordinary price of admission to every skill that is worth having.

Grace's neighbour Dev grows tomatoes in large pots on his balcony, and he checks on them every morning before he does anything else. A living thing that depends on you gives the day a very gentle sort of structure, and the reward of a ripening fruit is one that you can taste. Even a single pot of herbs on a window sill can do the same.

For many people, a dog or cat is a wonderful reason to get up in the morning, since an animal that is hungry or hopeful will not accept excuses. A pet is a large and long commitment, however, so think carefully, and be honest about the time, money and energy that you can truly offer. If a pet is not possible in your home, you could volunteer to walk a neighbour's dog or help at a local animal shelter.

Kofi works up the courage to ask his manager whether he might learn to use the warehouse's stock computer system, half expecting to be refused. A few weeks later he is being trusted with new tasks, and the same job that once felt like a treadmill now feels like a place where he is going somewhere. Sometimes a reason is hiding inside the work that you already have, and it only needs a little courage and a question to bring it out.

Money worries are real, and it would be foolish to pretend that they do not make everything feel harder. Even so, many of the finest reasons to get up cost nothing at all, such as a walk by the river, a long chat with a neighbour or a borrowed library book. A pleasant day is not always an expensive one, and the best moments are often the ones that nobody could ever have charged you for.

Take a calendar and choose one thing to look forward to in each month of the coming year. They may be modest, such as a picnic, a film or a visit to a friend, but together they give the year a series of bright landmarks that you can see from a long way off. Anticipation is a cheap and very effective form of happiness, and it can be enjoyed for weeks before the event itself arrives.

A wish is far more likely to come true once it has a date beside it, so do not leave your plans floating in the vague future. Circle the day on the calendar, tell a friend about it, and you will feel its pull growing stronger as it approaches. A date turns a hope into an appointment, and appointments are hard to ignore.

Before you go to sleep each night, write down three good things that happened during the day, however tiny they may seem. A friendly stranger, a perfect slice of toast or a sudden patch of blue sky all count, and within a week or two you will find yourself noticing such things as they happen. What you look for, you tend to find, so it is worth training your eyes to search for something kind.

People are sometimes told, or tell themselves, that they are too old to begin something new, and it is true that a few things do become harder with age. Nevertheless, at almost any age it remains possible to learn, to make new friends and to enjoy the thrill of a fresh start, as every adult education class demonstrates. The question is rarely whether you can begin, but whether you will allow yourself to, and that decision belongs entirely to you.

Grace begins to give short talks about garden birds at the library, and the audience asks her thoughtful, delightful questions. She realises that she is still a teacher at heart, only now she teaches because she wants to rather than because a timetable demands it. Retirement ended her job, but it did not end the thing she was good at.

There will be mornings when you stay in bed all the same, and that is not a catastrophe, nor proof that nothing works. Do not scold yourself, which only makes the next morning heavier, but simply decide that you will try again tomorrow with one small reason ready beside the bed. Progress is made of many fresh starts rather than of an unbroken streak, and nobody who has ever improved has done so perfectly.

If you feel that nothing interests you for many weeks, or if your sleep, appetite and energy have changed a great deal, please speak to a doctor. Low mood is common and often treatable, and asking for help is a sensible act rather than a sign of weakness, since this book is general encouragement and cannot replace medical advice. You deserve proper support, and it is available, so please do not feel that you have to carry this quietly by yourself.

One afternoon Grace and Kofi meet at a bus stop, and in the middle of a conversation about the weather Kofi admits that he finds the mornings hard. Grace tells him, with a smile, that she does too, and that simple honesty turns out to be a relief for both of them. A struggle that is spoken aloud very often turns out to be shared, and sharing it makes it a little lighter for everyone.

A reason that works beautifully in spring may have faded by autumn, and that is no cause for alarm. Take your list out every few months, drop whatever has lost its pull, and add something fresh, much as a gardener changes what grows in each season. A life with a living list of reasons is more resilient than a life with a single, fixed one.

Let us gather the ideas of this book into one place before we part. Look for small reasons rather than grand ones, share your days with other people, stay curious, set goals that are gentle enough to meet, and rest without apology when you are tired. None of this is difficult, but all of it gets easier when you begin.

Tonight, before you turn out the light, choose one small reason to get up tomorrow and say it aloud, even if it only concerns a cup of tea or a walk to the corner. In the morning the alarm will ring exactly as before, but this time you will have something on the other side of it that is waiting for you. That, quietly and without any fuss, is how nearly every good day begins, and tomorrow's can begin that way for you.
